notes:
I found verse-by-verse comment for every verse. I couldn't find any denominational disagreement over this chapter, any prosperity or word-of-faith teaching on it, or any notes from bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org or oca.org, so those are left out.

**v. 1**
- In 1 Kings 2:46 the kingdom is "established in the hands of Solomon" after Adonijah's death. Andrew Hill links "established himself" to the steps Solomon took to secure the throne in 1 Kings 2. God being "with" Solomon echoes what was said of David. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-1-commentary
- Raymond Dillard notes that the verb "exalted" is also used twice of Joshua. He suggests Moses handing over to Joshua is the model for David handing over to Solomon. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-1-commentary
- Ron Daniel's point: Adonijah tried to exalt himself and was brought down; it was the Lord who exalted Solomon. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/64184/
- The Targum renders "the LORD was with him" as "The WORD of the Lord was his support." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-chronicles/1-1.html

**v. 2**
- Ellicott: "the chief of the fathers" means the heads of the clans, and it explains the phrase before it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/1.htm
- A commentary quoted on Bible Hub (not named in the excerpt I saw) says the leaders were called to a solemn religious procession, dated to Solomon's second year. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/1-5.htm
- Matthew Henry: the king's great men should join him in worshipping God, and opening his reign with this public visit to God's altar was a good sign. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-1-commentary

**v. 3**
- Pulpit Commentary: "all the congregation" means the people as represented by their captains, judges, princes and family heads. It thinks David moved the tabernacle to Gibeon, probably right after Saul destroyed Nob. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/1-3.htm
- Ellicott translates "God's tent of meeting," meaning meeting with man. G. Campbell Morgan (quoted by Guzik) agrees: it was where the people met with God, not with each other. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/1.htm ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-1/
- **Was worship at a "high place" right?** Commentators differ:
  - Cambridge Bible: the Chronicler defends this high-place worship by explaining that the Tabernacle stood there. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/1-3.htm
  - Constable says the Gibeon tabernacle was still a legitimate place of worship. Grant sees no scriptural objection to this high place at the time. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-chronicles/1-3.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/2-chronicles-1.html
  - Ron Daniel, by contrast, says the site was on a high place, which was not pleasing to God, because it followed the model of the Canaanite offerings. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/64184/
  - Ligonier (Reformed) holds that Solomon's loyalty was already divided early in his reign, pointing to his marriage to Pharaoh's daughter. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/solomons-wise-request

**v. 4**
- The tabernacle and bronze altar stayed at Gibeon, but David had taken the ark out and put it in a tent in Jerusalem. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/64184/
- One study note says having the tent at Gibeon and the ark in Jerusalem suggests two different, major religious centers prior to the construction of the Jerusalem temple. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/64184/
- Guzik (citing Morgan): God met Solomon at Gibeon even though the ark wasn't there. His presence was not to be superstitiously tied to the ark. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-1/
- Grant sees an inconsistency in the ark not being present, because the ark stands for Christ's authority. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/2-chronicles-1.html

**v. 5**
- Ellicott reads "was there" rather than "he put," a one-letter difference in the Hebrew. On his reading the old bronze altar is what made Gibeon the legitimate place of sacrifice. He also translates the end of the verse as "sought Him," meaning the Lord. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/1.htm
- Konkel (citing Dillard): Solomon is modelled on Bezalel. Only after seeking God at Bezalel's altar is he given wisdom. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-1-commentary
- Guzik reads the altar as the place of atoning sacrifice. Coming there was the Old Testament equivalent to coming to the cross. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-1/
- GotQuestions (quoted on Precept Austin) calls the bronze altar a shadow of Christ, who took our judgment. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-1-commentary

**v. 6**
- Coffman: Solomon supplied the offerings; the priests actually offered them. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/2-chronicles-1.html
- Precept Austin says "a thousand" could simply be a hyperbole for many, many offerings. Mabie sees it as a visible sign of Solomon's reverence. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-1-commentary ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/64184/
- Matthew Henry: Solomon took his sacrifices to the altar, for it is the altar that sanctifieth every gift. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-1-commentary

**v. 7**
- Ellicott notes that 1 Kings calls this "a dream of the night." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/1.htm
- Guzik: God's offer wasn't only because of the 1,000 sacrifices; it was because Solomon's heart was surrendered. He also quotes Selman: the problem for many Christians is whether they will ask at all. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-1/
- A background note says that in ancient royal dreams like this, the dream validates the kingship or a planned undertaking. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/64184/

**v. 8**
- Guzik: before asking for anything, Solomon remembered God's faithfulness to David and to himself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-1/

**v. 9**
- Matthew Henry: wisdom wasn't one of the things promised to David, but it was needed to bring about what was promised, namely building God's house and establishing the throne. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-chronicles/1-1.html
- Mabie (as quoted on Precept Austin): Solomon asks for two things, that the covenant with David be fulfilled and that he be given wisdom. He sees himself as part of the promise to David. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/64184/

**v. 10**
- Guzik: "go out and come in" is a Hebrew expression meaning "That I may fulfill my duties before this people." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-1/
- J.A. Thompson: the request admits Solomon's own weakness and that Israel was God's people, not Solomon's. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-1-commentary
- Constable: Solomon wanted the wisdom to understand and obey the Law of Moses, which Israel's kings were to use in shepherding the nation. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-chronicles/1-1.html
- The Gospel Coalition: the request is more than unselfishness. As the son of David, Solomon asked for wisdom to build God's temple. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/solomon-ask-wisdom/

**v. 11**
- Guzik: God was pleased by what Solomon asked for and by what he didn't ask for. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-1/
- Ron Daniel warns that too many people ask God for stuff with the wrong motives. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-1-commentary

**v. 12**
- Guzik quotes Morgan: this was the overflowing grace of God; everything Solomon set aside for wisdom was also given to him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-1/
- Guzik also asks whether this was the best Solomon could have asked for. He quotes Maclaren: "There is no sign in his biography that he ever had the deep inward devotion of his father." He concludes that Solomon wasted these gifts. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-1/
- Hill sees a cue for the community after the exile: they too might receive similar gifts from God through prayer. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-1-commentary
- Several sources link this verse to James 1:5. Precept Austin adds "But ask in faith!" https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/64184/

**v. 13**
- Ellicott: the Hebrew literally says "came to the high place… to Jerusalem." "From the high place" should be read, as the Septuagint has it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/1.htm
- Matthew Henry: Solomon did no act of government until he had worshipped. It was first the tabernacle, and then the throne. And he didn't bury his gift but got on with ruling. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Ch/2Ch_001.cfm
- Guzik points to the judgment between the two mothers (1 Kings 3:16–28) as an example of this wisdom. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-1/

**v. 14**
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: "a prohibited indulgence, whether as an instrument of luxury or power." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/1-16.htm
- Guzik: Solomon's stables show he didn't take God's word seriously enough, since Deuteronomy 17:16 says the king shall not multiply horses. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-1/
- TGC calls the army large for its day. Its note says "1,200 chariots," although the ESV text on the same page says 1,400, so the 1,200 looks like a slip. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/2-chronicles/

**v. 15**
- Guzik: the Chronicler expects readers to know Deuteronomy 17:17, "nor shall he greatly multiply silver and gold for himself." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-1/
- Matthew Henry: more gold lowers its value, but more grace raises it. How much better to get wisdom than gold! https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/64184/
- Hill: the reports of Solomon's wealth here and in chapter 9 act as bookends around the temple-building story. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-1-commentary

**v. 16**
- **"Kue":** the KJV has "linen yarn." The Cambridge Bible says that word may instead be a place name known from Assyrian inscriptions, Kuë (Cilicia). It adds that Egypt was probably only the market, not where the horses were raised. Ellicott reads the word as "company" or "drove." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/1-16.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: "linen yarn" is without doubt wrong. The Vulgate (the Latin Bible used by Catholics) reads "from Coa," perhaps meaning Tekoa. https://biblehub.com/2_chronicles/1-16.htm
- Guzik calls this verse a "dark note." He suggests Solomon may have rationalised it as trading on behalf of others. It started a chain: an Egyptian wife, many foreign wives, temples to their gods, and finally idolatry. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-1/
- TGC: God didn't want his people doing anything that restored contact with Egypt, the land they were rescued from as slaves. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/2-chronicles/

**v. 17**
- JFB: a chariot cost four times as much as a horse. The Syrians could only import Egyptian horses through Judea, so Solomon established a monopoly. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/1-16.htm
- TGC: Solomon bought at wholesale rates from Egypt and Kue and resold to surrounding nations. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/2-chronicles/

**Other views**
- **Catholic (vv. 7–12):** Catholic Bibles include the Book of Wisdom, whose chapter 9 is a longer version of Solomon's prayer for wisdom. Catholic.com says the writer speaks in Solomon's name, a device it calls pseudonymity. It notes that the book stresses wisdom is to be sought through prayer, because we cannot attain it by our own efforts. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/wisdom ; text at https://www.newadvent.org/bible/wis009.htm
- **About the book (Ellicott's introduction):** Ellicott calls the Hebrew text of Chronicles in an unsatisfactory condition. That's why he suggests corrections in vv. 5, 6 and 13. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/1.htm
